name: the nameless city
aliases: this hoary survivor of the deluge
this great-grandmother of the eldest pyramid
facts: It protrudes uncannily above the desert sands as parts of a corpse might protrude from an ill-made grave.
Fear spoke from its age-worn stones, called a hoary survivor of the deluge and great-grandmother of the eldest pyramid.
It lies remote in the desert of Araby, crumbling and inarticulate, its low walls nearly hidden by sands of uncounted ages.
There is no legend so old as to give it a name or recall that it was ever alive.
All the tribes shun it without wholly knowing why.
Abdul Alhazred the mad poet dreamed of this place the night before composing his couplet.
The narrator alone of living men has seen it.
Its ruins consist of shapeless foundations of houses and palaces with no carving or inscription found.
A low cliff nearby had hewn facades of several small, squat rock houses or temples.
One cavern proved to be a temple with primitive altars, pillars, and niches, all curiously low, and stones shaped into symbols.
A larger temple was presumably a natural cavern since it bore winds from some region beyond, and had traces of pictorial art and curvilinear carvings on its altars.

On the walls and roof I beheld for the first time some traces of the pictorial art of the ancient race

name: The Narrator
facts: He was traveling in a parched and terrible valley under the moon when he first saw the nameless city.
He alone has seen the nameless city, and no other face bears such hideous lines of fear as his.
No other man shivers so horribly as he does when the night wind rattles the windows.
He defied the Arabs' warnings and went into the untrodden waste with his camel.
He had many tools and dug much within the walls of the obliterated edifices.
He cleared a sand-choked aperture with his spade and crawled through it, carrying a torch, to enter a temple.

name: Abdul Alhazred
facts: He dreamed of the nameless city the night before he sang his unexplainable couplet.
He is credited with the couplet: 'That is not dead which can eternal lie, And with strange eons, even death may die.'
